articles.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
articles.content:
A massive galaxy cluster dating back to an era when such enormous structures were only beginning to take shape is challenging scientists' understanding of how the universe evolved. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) reveal that the cluster contains an unusually dense concentration of matter, suggesting that some cosmic structures may have developed much faster than current models predict.

The galaxy cluster, known as XLSSC 122, has become the focus of three recent studies led by researchers at IPAC, Caltech's science and data center for astrophysics and planetary science. Their findings establish XLSSC 122 as the most distant galaxy cluster known to exhibit strong gravitational lensing, a phenomenon that allows astronomers to measure the mass of otherwise invisible matter. The research was presented at a press conference on June 17, 2026, during the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society.

Located approximately 10.4 billion light-years from Earth, XLSSC 122 stood out to astronomers because of its surprising maturity. Although it existed during a period when galaxy clusters were still assembling, it already displayed the size and organized structure typically associated with clusters in the modern universe.

Webb has now uncovered another remarkable feature. XLSSC 122 happens to lie directly in front of one or more galaxies that are even farther away. The cluster's powerful gravity bends and distorts the light traveling from those background galaxies, creating a rare effect called strong gravitational lensing. This fortunate alignment has given scientists an exceptionally precise way to measure how mass is distributed throughout the cluster.

"When we got those first images back from JWST, we said, 'wow, look at this, there's strong lensing coming from this cluster!'" said Kyle Finner, a staff scientist at IPAC and lead author of the first paper examining the cluster. "XLSSC 122 has now set the record for the most distant galaxy cluster displaying strong lensing, which is a valuable tool for astronomers."

An Ancient Galaxy Cluster Challenges Cosmic Predictions

The newly detected gravitational lensing has allowed researchers to examine the distribution of mass in an ancient galaxy cluster in greater detail than ever before. XLSSC 122 dates to a period known as "cosmic noon," roughly 10 billion years ago, when the universe was experiencing its most intense era of star formation.

During this time, galaxies were producing stars at rates up to 100 times higher than those observed in the present-day universe. Galaxy clusters were also becoming increasingly common as smaller systems gradually combined into larger structures.

Yet XLSSC 122 appears to have developed in an unexpected way. The new measurements show that a remarkably large amount of its mass is packed into its central region. According to standard cosmological models, the growth of massive structures should have been more gradual, making such a concentrated cluster particularly surprising at this early stage of cosmic history.

"XLSSC 122 is one of the first clusters we know of that formed in the universe, and it has a mass concentration that doesn't agree with our cosmological model predictions," said Finner.

To investigate the mystery further, Finner and his collaborators conducted two additional JWST studies, first authored by Zachary Scofield and Hyungjin Joo at Yonsei University. Together, the three papers provide a much more complete picture of this unusual cluster and offer new insights into galaxy cluster formation during cosmic noon.

James Webb Reveals Hidden Dark Matter

Astronomers originally identified XLSSC 122 in 2014 through an X-ray survey carried out by the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton spacecraft. Later observations with the Hubble Space Telescope helped establish its distance of approximately 10.4 billion light-years and confirmed that the cluster appeared unusually developed for its age.

However, Hubble did not reveal clear evidence of strong gravitational lensing. That changed when JWST captured distinctive curved arcs of light surrounding the cluster's center, providing the first definitive signs of this phenomenon in XLSSC 122.

"Before JWST, we couldn't do this level of science in the early, distant universe," said Finner.

The gravitational distortions are caused primarily by something astronomers cannot directly observe: dark matter.

Although XLSSC 122 contains visible stars and glowing gas, these familiar forms of matter account for only a small fraction of the gravitational lensing effect. Most of the distortion comes from dark matter, an invisible substance that has not been directly detected through light but whose gravitational influence is supported by extensive astronomical evidence.

Scientists estimate that dark matter is approximately five times more abundant than ordinary matter, which makes up stars, planets, and everything around us. Its gravity helps hold galaxies together and shapes the universe's enormous network of galaxy groups, clusters, and filaments.

Because dark matter plays such an important role in cosmic structure, determining how it was distributed billions of years ago offers a powerful way to test theories describing the universe's development since the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

"Strong lensing is a way to measure the dark matter without actually seeing the dark matter," said Finner. "It gives us a sensitive probe of our cosmological models."

A Wider View Reveals a Galaxy Cluster Merger

In their second paper, the researchers investigated XLSSC 122 using another form of gravitational lensing known as weak lensing.

Strong gravitational lensing produces obvious distortions, including the striking arcs captured by JWST. Weak lensing, by comparison, causes much smaller changes in the apparent shapes of distant galaxies. These subtle effects are difficult to identify individually, so astronomers rely on statistical methods to detect them.

The two techniques provide complementary information. Strong lensing is especially useful for measuring the mass concentrated near a cluster's center, while weak lensing can reveal how matter is distributed across its outer regions.

"Weak gravitational lensing can constrain mass much further out, so you can get a better picture of the surrounding cluster area," said Finner.

By combining these measurements with X-ray and radio observations from other telescopes, the scientists determined that XLSSC 122 is still undergoing a merger. Its galaxies are continuing to come together as the larger cluster takes shape.

The broader analysis also reinforced the earlier finding that an unusually large amount of mass is concentrated near the cluster's center.

Ancient Starlight Offers New Clues to Dark Matter

The team's third and most recent paper revealed another important feature of XLSSC 122: faint light produced by stars that are no longer bound to individual galaxies.

Known as intracluster light, this diffuse glow comes from stars scattered into the spaces between galaxies. Webb's observations represent the earliest known detection of intracluster light, providing another way to examine the development of galaxy clusters in the distant universe.

The widespread distribution of this light supports the conclusion that XLSSC 122 is undergoing a merger. As galaxies interact and collide, some stars are pulled away from their original galaxies and spread throughout the cluster. In XLSSC 122, many of these displaced stars appear not to have settled into its dense central region.

The researchers also uncovered an intriguing connection between these wandering stars and dark matter.

Near the cluster's center, the shape of the intracluster light closely matches the distribution of dark matter inferred from strong gravitational lensing. This suggests that the faint glow of stars between galaxies could potentially serve as a visible indicator of where invisible dark matter is concentrated.

If astronomers observe the same relationship in other clusters, particularly those from the early universe, intracluster light could become a valuable new tool for mapping dark matter across cosmic history.

"In this cluster, the intracluster light essentially traces the dark matter," said Finner. "That light tells us that the cluster is in a merging state."

Could More Ancient Galaxy Clusters Challenge Cosmology?

The next goal for Finner and his colleagues is to identify and investigate dozens of additional galaxy clusters from similarly early periods in the universe's history.

Finding these distant objects requires a different approach from studying them in detail. Although JWST is exceptionally powerful, its relatively narrow field of view makes it better suited to examining selected targets than searching enormous areas of the sky.

Instead, astronomers must first identify promising candidates through wide-area X-ray and radio surveys, similar to the observations that originally revealed XLSSC 122.

One promising technique relies on the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, which occurs when energetic particles inside galaxy clusters scatter radiation from the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang.

This interaction can create distinctive regions that appear as "holes" in observations of the cosmic microwave background. By searching for these signatures, astronomers can locate galaxy clusters that might otherwise be difficult to detect.

Finding more objects like XLSSC 122 could have major implications for cosmology. If other ancient clusters also contain unexpectedly concentrated dark matter and display unusually advanced development, scientists may need to revise some of their basic assumptions about how quickly large cosmic structures formed.

For now, XLSSC 122 provides an important test of existing models, but a larger sample will be necessary to determine whether its unusual properties are rare or part of a broader pattern in the early universe.

"It's still early in the JWST era," said Finner, "and if we can start to get data on tens or hundreds of these types of objects at this stage in the universe, then we can really start putting our cosmological models to the test."

articles.personality_title: James Webb uncovers a distant galaxy cluster that challenges cosmic history
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists study galaxy clusters to understand how the universe formed over billions of years. Galaxy clusters are groups of galaxies held together by gravity, often containing large amounts of dark matter, which cannot be seen but affects how galaxies move.

**What happened** – NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) discovered a very old galaxy cluster called XLSSC 122, about 10.4 billion light-years away. This cluster is unusually dense and mature for its age. JWST observed strong gravitational lensing, where the cluster’s gravity bends light from even more distant galaxies. This effect lets scientists measure the cluster’s mass, especially its dark matter.

**Impact** – XLSSC 122 is the most distant cluster known to show strong gravitational lensing. Its dense core and the way stars are spread out challenge current ideas about how fast such big structures formed in the early universe. The discovery also revealed that faint light from stars floating between galaxies matches the dark matter’s shape, offering a new way to study invisible dark matter.

**What's next step** – Researchers aim to find many more ancient galaxy clusters using wide-area surveys and special techniques like the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect. Studying more clusters like XLSSC 122 will help confirm if its unusual features are common and may lead scientists to update their models about the universe’s growth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – James Webb’s discovery of a massive, mature galaxy cluster billions of years old provides new clues about dark matter and how the universe’s largest structures formed faster than expected.
articles.personality_title_fr: James Webb révèle un amas de galaxies lointain qui remet en question l’histoire cosmique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient les amas de galaxies pour comprendre comment l’univers s’est formé au cours des milliards d’années. Les amas de galaxies sont des groupes de galaxies maintenus ensemble par la gravité, souvent riches en matière noire, une substance invisible qui influence le mouvement des galaxies.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le télescope spatial James Webb (JWST) de la NASA a découvert un très vieil amas de galaxies appelé XLSSC 122, situé à environ 10,4 milliards d’années-lumière. Cet amas est étonnamment dense et mature pour son âge. JWST a observé un fort effet de lentille gravitationnelle, où la gravité de l’amas déforme la lumière d’autres galaxies encore plus lointaines. Cet effet permet aux scientifiques de mesurer la masse de l’amas, notamment sa matière noire.

**Impact** – XLSSC 122 est l’amas le plus lointain connu à présenter un fort effet de lentille gravitationnelle. Son noyau dense et la répartition des étoiles remettent en cause les idées actuelles sur la vitesse de formation de telles structures dans l’univers primitif. La découverte a aussi montré que la lumière faible des étoiles entre les galaxies correspond à la forme de la matière noire, offrant une nouvelle méthode pour étudier cette matière invisible.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent trouver beaucoup plus d’amas de galaxies anciens grâce à des relevés étendus et des techniques spéciales comme l’effet Sunyaev-Zel'dovich. Étudier plus d’amas comme XLSSC 122 aidera à savoir si ses caractéristiques inhabituelles sont courantes et pourrait amener à revoir les modèles sur la croissance de l’univers.

**Résumé en une phrase** – La découverte par James Webb d’un amas de galaxies massif et mature vieux de milliards d’années apporte de nouveaux indices sur la matière noire et la formation rapide des plus grandes structures de l’univers.
articles.personality_title_es: James Webb descubre un cúmulo de galaxias distante que desafía la historia cósmica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos estudian los cúmulos de galaxias para entender cómo se formó el universo durante miles de millones de años. Un cúmulo de galaxias es un grupo de galaxias unidas por la gravedad, que a menudo contienen grandes cantidades de materia oscura, una sustancia invisible que afecta el movimiento de las galaxias.

**Qué pasó** – El telescopio espacial James Webb (JWST) de la NASA descubrió un cúmulo de galaxias muy antiguo llamado XLSSC 122, que se encuentra a unos 10.4 mil millones de años luz. Este cúmulo es sorprendentemente denso y maduro para su edad. JWST observó un fuerte efecto de lente gravitacional, donde la gravedad del cúmulo dobla la luz de galaxias aún más lejanas. Este efecto permite a los científicos medir la masa del cúmulo, especialmente su materia oscura.

**Impacto** – XLSSC 122 es el cúmulo más lejano conocido que muestra un fuerte efecto de lente gravitacional. Su núcleo denso y la forma en que están distribuidas las estrellas desafían las ideas actuales sobre la velocidad con la que se formaron estas grandes estructuras en el universo temprano. El descubrimiento también mostró que la luz débil de estrellas entre las galaxias coincide con la forma de la materia oscura, ofreciendo una nueva forma de estudiar esta materia invisible.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores buscan encontrar muchos más cúmulos de galaxias antiguos mediante estudios amplios y técnicas especiales como el efecto Sunyaev-Zel'dovich. Estudiar más cúmulos como XLSSC 122 ayudará a confirmar si sus características inusuales son comunes y podría llevar a actualizar los modelos sobre el crecimiento del universo.

**Resumen en una frase** – El descubrimiento de James Webb de un cúmulo de galaxias masivo y maduro hace miles de millones de años ofrece nuevas pistas sobre la materia oscura y cómo se formaron más rápido de lo esperado las estructuras más grandes del universo.

articles.title: Will we observe dark matter as a particle or a wave?
articles.summary: We have arguably already discovered dark matter, says columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein. To observe it, we will need to figure out whether we expect it to act like a particle or a wave.
articles.content:
We have arguably already discovered dark matter, says columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein. To observe it, we will need to figure out whether we expect it to act like a particle or a wave.

Part of the Lux-Zeplin detector at the Sanford Underground Research Facility Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility

A few years ago, I was working on a document that would be read by US policymakers, and we had some internal discussion about how to frame our goal. Should we say that we are hoping to discover dark matter? No, we ultimately concluded, because we had, in fact, already done that. We have already discovered dark matter using multiple types of astrophysical observation, including the motions of stars in galaxies, which indicate the presence of an apparently invisible matter-like phenomenon that interacts through gravity and not noticeably through any other force. When we look at light from the dawn of time, when it flew freely through the universe, we can only match our observations with cosmological theories if we assume that dark matter exists.

We realised that what we really wanted to say is that we want to figure out what dark matter is. We already know that most of the normally gravitating matter in the universe is an invisible substance that outnumbers visible matter at a rate of about five to one. While this is useful information, it hardly tells us much detail, and many particle physics theories can account for these astrophysical observations. So, the question becomes how we tell the difference between the many different dark matter models. And to sort that out, the devil is in the details.

Certainly, one approach is to look for evidence of dark matter interactions here on Earth. You may have seen recent news items about the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, which announced a single data point that could represent a dark matter particle interacting with atomic nuclei. If this result bears out – and it is a long way off from being statistically significant – it would represent the first evidence that dark matter interacts via nuclear forces. It would also be our most direct look at what dark matter is.

Advertisement

In the absence of substantive data in the lab, we remain dependent on astrophysical observations. In this case, we have to figure out how to use data that seems to be, on the surface, consistent with different hypothetical particles that could be making up dark matter. For example, LZ is looking for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs). Meanwhile, I spend most of my research time focused on a category of particles with a very different set of characteristics from WIMPs, called axions. While WIMPs will manifest in a particle-like way in galaxies, axions are more likely to behave as waves. This is a reflection of the principle of wave-particle duality, which tells us that all particles are also waves from the point of view of quantum physics. With axions, their wave-like nature is expected to visibly manifest across astrophysical data, including observations of dwarf galaxies and the cosmic microwave background radiation. Their signature should sometimes look different from what we would expect to see with WIMPs.

To have a chance at figuring out whether dark matter is made of axions rather than WIMPs, we first have to run computer simulations that project what the data might look like for one or the other. Only then can we see if our observations match. And we often have to make simplifying assumptions in order to do our calculations; here’s where the devil shows up.

In two new preprints that I published in September with Hoang Nhan Luu at the University of New Hampshire, we study an axion model that pushes past the simplifying assumptions that are common in our research community. Our work shows that this model – developed by an international team that includes some former colleagues from MIT – may both make simulations go faster and make them more accurate. This kind of work is unlikely to make headlines, but it does what science needs it to do. It helps create the conditions where we will finally move past discovering dark matter, to truly understanding it.

It highlights ongoing research and experiments like LUX-ZEPLIN that could provide direct evidence of dark matter's nature, which would have broad implications for our understanding of the universe. The article provides sufficient detail on the approaches and challenges involved, making it a substantive and inspiring scientific advancement with wide-reaching impact.
articles.personality_title: Scientists close in on understanding dark matter as particle or wave
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dark matter is a mysterious substance that makes up most of the matter in the universe. Scientists have seen its effects in space but have not yet directly observed what it actually is. 

**What happened** – Researchers, including those working on the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, are trying to detect dark matter on Earth. LZ recently found a possible sign of dark matter interacting with atoms, but more proof is needed. Meanwhile, scientists study two main ideas: dark matter could be made of particles called WIMPs, which act like tiny solid objects, or axions, which behave more like waves.

**Impact** – Understanding if dark matter acts like a particle or a wave will help scientists know what it really is. This is important because it changes how we study the universe and could explain many cosmic mysteries. New computer simulations are improving how researchers test these ideas, making the search more accurate and faster.

**What's next step** – Scientists will keep running detailed simulations and analyzing data from experiments like LZ. They aim to match their models with real observations, which could soon reveal the true nature of dark matter.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Researchers are making progress in identifying dark matter by studying whether it behaves like particles or waves, bringing us closer to understanding the universe’s hidden mass.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques se rapprochent de la compréhension de la matière noire comme particule ou onde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La matière noire est une substance mystérieuse qui compose la majorité de la matière dans l’univers. Les scientifiques ont observé ses effets dans l’espace, mais n’ont pas encore directement vu ce qu’elle est réellement.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs, dont ceux de l’expérience LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ), tentent de détecter la matière noire sur Terre. LZ a récemment trouvé un indice possible d’interaction de la matière noire avec des atomes, mais il faut encore des preuves supplémentaires. En même temps, les scientifiques étudient deux idées principales : la matière noire pourrait être composée de particules appelées WIMPs, qui agissent comme de petits objets solides, ou d’axions, qui se comportent plutôt comme des ondes.

**Impact** – Comprendre si la matière noire agit comme une particule ou une onde aidera les scientifiques à savoir ce qu’elle est vraiment. C’est important car cela change notre façon d’étudier l’univers et pourrait expliquer de nombreux mystères cosmiques. De nouvelles simulations informatiques améliorent la manière dont les chercheurs testent ces idées, rendant la recherche plus précise et rapide.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à exécuter des simulations détaillées et à analyser les données des expériences comme LZ. Ils espèrent faire correspondre leurs modèles aux observations réelles, ce qui pourrait bientôt révéler la vraie nature de la matière noire.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les chercheurs progressent dans l’identification de la matière noire en étudiant si elle se comporte comme des particules ou des ondes, nous rapprochant de la compréhension de la masse cachée de l’univers.
articles.personality_title_es: Los científicos avanzan en entender la materia oscura como partícula u onda
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La materia oscura es una sustancia misteriosa que compone la mayor parte de la materia en el universo. Los científicos han visto sus efectos en el espacio, pero aún no han observado directamente qué es.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores, incluidos los que trabajan en el experimento LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ), están intentando detectar la materia oscura en la Tierra. LZ encontró recientemente una posible señal de materia oscura interactuando con átomos, pero se necesita más evidencia. Mientras tanto, los científicos estudian dos ideas principales: la materia oscura podría estar hecha de partículas llamadas WIMPs, que actúan como pequeños objetos sólidos, o axiones, que se comportan más como ondas.

**Impacto** – Entender si la materia oscura actúa como partícula u onda ayudará a los científicos a saber qué es realmente. Esto es importante porque cambia cómo estudiamos el universo y podría explicar muchos misterios cósmicos. Nuevas simulaciones por computadora están mejorando cómo los investigadores prueban estas ideas, haciendo la búsqueda más rápida y precisa.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán realizando simulaciones detalladas y analizando datos de experimentos como LZ. Esperan comparar sus modelos con observaciones reales, lo que podría revelar pronto la verdadera naturaleza de la materia oscura.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los investigadores avanzan en identificar la materia oscura estudiando si se comporta como partículas u ondas, acercándonos a entender la masa oculta del universo.
